🐫 Happy Wednesday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,499 words ... 5½ mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

🏛️ Driving the day: In a court filing ahead of an emergency hearing today, the Trump administration defends expelling CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, arguing that the government has a compelling interest in awarding press passes "to journalists satisfying minimum standards."

  • In a joint statement, the three outlets said they were suing "to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes." NYT gift link.
 
 
1 big thing: The "All-In"-ization of Trump
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine increasingly bears the stamp of the "All-In" podcasters, whose tech-investor network now feeds ideas and talent directly into the White House, Axios' Zachary Basu writes.

  • Why it matters: An unlikely marriage of convenience between MAGA and Silicon Valley has proved remarkably durable, deepening as Trump sheds support elsewhere and stakes more of his legacy on dominating the AI race.

The big picture: "All-In," now including lucrative events and luxe tequila, is a smash hit that grew out of four hyperconnected tech entrepreneurs kibitzing on air during COVID, when they could no longer gather for their weekly poker game. The co-hosts, who call themselves "The Besties," are Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, and David Friedberg.

  • None of them has done more to bridge the two worlds than David Sacks, who spent Trump's first year as his AI czar and remains a powerful outside adviser with direct access to the president.
  • Sacks helped build Trump's original AI agenda around a simple premise: Move fast, sweep away regulatory barriers and treat China — not catastrophic risk — as the overriding threat.

🔭 Zoom out: Sacks left the White House but not Trump's inner circle, shaping AI policy as co-chair of the Trump-created President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST). The broader "All-In" network is embedding itself deeper across Trumpworld:

  • David Friedberg also serves on the science council, alongside investor Marc Andreessen, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other tech leaders.
  • Chamath Palihapitiya, another co-host and prominent Trump booster, is among the names being floated for the new AI czar job Trump announced last weekend.

The intrigue: The show routinely defends Trump. Jason Calacanis, the moderator, is the political outlier — frequently criticizing Trump on Iran and inflation, while otherwise aligning with his co-hosts on the revolutionary nature of AI.

President Trump speaks at the UN General Assembly in Manhattan yesterday. Photo: Brendan Smialowski/Getty Images

👓 Between the lines: Few platforms better capture the zeitgeist of AI accelerationism than "All-In," where the movement's leading investors, executives and political allies increasingly converge.

  • After former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's safety warnings exploded across Washington, the hosts devoted much of their next episode to portraying the backlash as an orchestrated "doomer" campaign.
  • Three days later, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang paused his live "All-In" Summit interview to take a call from Trump, who drew a raucous reception as he dismissed AI catastrophe fears as a "hoax."

👀 What to watch: "All-In" and the accelerationist wing of Silicon Valley are tying themselves unusually tightly to one president and one governing philosophy.

  • Sacks has blessed a $100 million-plus midterm operation built to advance Trump's AI agenda and punish candidates who favor tougher regulation.
  • Inside AI labs, that political fusion is feeding a deeper fear: that warnings about catastrophic risk will become coded as anti-Trump politics, turning AI safety into yet another partisan litmus test.

2. 🦾 New AI models tout affordability
 

Illustration: Eniola Odetunde/Axios
 

Cheaper, more powerful AI models could pave the way for top labs to safely slow development without going broke, Axios' Madison Mills writes.

  • Why it matters: OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs have said they want to slow the pace of development. But as long as frontier models require ever-larger spending, the pressure to keep racing may be too strong to resist.

🖼️ The big picture: The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will for the foreseeable future.

  • To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable.

🔬 Zoom in: This week brought a spate of new models. One thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever, without forgoing top intelligence.

  • OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago.

3. ⚡ Scoop: $2B Gaza recovery plan
 
Workers search the rubble of a Gaza City building that collapsed last week. It had been damaged by an Israeli strike earlier in the war. Photo: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters

President Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members today, Axios' Barak Ravid reports from New York.

  • Why it matters: The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war reconstruction and governance in Gaza would look like.

The plan includes money for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, according to a copy obtained by Axios.

  • The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade.
  • A Board of Peace official said that "the plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster."

🥊 Reality check: For the plan to work, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate.

  • While Bibi's government agreed in principle to aspects of the plan that were previously discussed, Israel refused to start implementing it, mainly for domestic political reasons ahead of next month's elections.
  • And while Hamas has agreed in principle to disarm, that pledge hasn't been tested.

4. ⚖️ Poll: Americans say rule of law is declining
 
Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Visuals

A majority of Americans (56%) say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, Axios' Margaret Talev writes from a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults.

  • 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution.
  • But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't.

5. 🚕 Uber's robotaxi edge: Human drivers
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers, Axios' Joann Muller writes.

  • Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis.

💡 How it works: In a hybrid network, AVs would handle the steady "base load" of everyday demand.

  • Human drivers would provide extra capacity during rush hour, bad weather, concerts and other demand spikes.

6. 🗳️ Trump amps up hunt for voter fraud
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photo: Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
 

The Trump administration says Americans should prepare between now and Election Day for a wave of new arrests and prosecutions over alleged noncitizen voter fraud, Axios' Brittany Gibson writes.

  • Why it matters: The Trump administration is deploying hundreds of federal investigators and attorneys to pursue President Trump's long-running fixation — and test a broader Republican claim that tougher enforcement will uncover far more illegal voting.

A Justice Department official told reporters yesterday that the "initiative is a tier one priority. It's a top priority for the attorney general and for the White House."

  • Across the country, there are now 1,600 open cases of potential voter fraud and 160 people have been arrested, a Homeland Security Investigations official said.
  • To support these investigations, Homeland Security staff have shifted work time from other priorities such as smuggling, trafficking and financial fraud.

Reality check: Instances of mistaken registrations and cases of noncitizen voting are rare, but they've long been investigated by the federal government.

7. 🎧 Charted: Music's new record
 
Data: Billboard. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

Country sensation Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" is now the longest-running No. 1 song in the Billboard Hot 100's history after spending 23 weeks in the top spot, Axios' Sara Fischer and Neal Rothschild write.

  • It passed Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," which accumulated 22 weeks at No. 1 across seven holiday seasons.

Between the lines: More songs are staying on the charts for longer as streaming algorithms encourage repeat listens and vertical video platforms serve as extended marketing tools.

8. 🐧 1 fun thing: Penguin acupuncture
 
Photo: New England Aquarium

New England Aquarium veterinarians are turning to acupuncture to help out their oldest penguin, Axios Boston's Mike Deehan writes.

  • Pip, a 29-year-old African penguin, has lived about twice as long as his species typically survives in the wild.

Staff noticed Pip's limp and altered gait late last year, and feared arthritis-related conditions common in older penguins.

  • After trying pain medication, vets added acupuncture and physical therapy from an outside specialist to Pip's routine.
